title: Asking questions
goal: Build questions with the full Malay toolkit — including three question markers that decide whether your question sounds formal, casual or blunt.
bekal: use *apa, siapa, mana, bila, kenapa, macam mana, berapa* in Malay word order
choose between *-kah*, *ke* and tone of voice to mark a question
soften questions so they don't sound like an interrogation

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Questions at the college counter
dialogs.intro: Sarah goes to the college office to collect her room key. The clerk at the counter asks her one question after another, and Sarah asks some back.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya nak ambil kunci bilik. Bilik dua belas.
lines.id: I'd like to collect my room key. Room twelve.
lines.literal: I want take key room. room two teen.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Sekejap… S dua kosong lapan tiga empat.
lines.id: Just a moment… S two zero eight three four.
lines.literal: moment… S two zero eight three four.

lines.speaker: Kerani:
lines.id: Are you an international student, miss?

lines.speaker: Kerani:
lines.id: When did you arrive in Malaysia, miss?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Tiga hari lepas. Encik, kunci ni kena pulangkan bila?
lines.id: Three days ago. Sir, when do I have to return this key?
lines.literal: three day past. sir, key this must return when?

lines.speaker: Kerani:
lines.text: Hujung semester. Kalau hilang, kena denda lima puluh ringgit.
lines.id: At the end of the semester. If you lose it, there's a fifty-ringgit fine.
lines.literal: end semester. if lost, get fine five ten ringgit.

lines.speaker: Kerani:
lines.text: Sebab kena tukar mangga pintu sekali. Jaga elok-elok ya.
lines.id: Because the door padlock has to be changed too. Take good care of it.
lines.literal: because must change padlock door together. guard well-well yes.

notes: **Adakah** is the **formal** question marker, placed at the **start** of a sentence, a bit like "Is it the case that…?": *Adakah cik pelajar antarabangsa?* In everyday speech it's hardly ever used — people say *Cik pelajar antarabangsa ke?* You need to **recognize** it (it appears on forms, in letters and at official counters), but you don't have to use it.

**Antarabangsa** = international, literally "between nations" (*antara* + *bangsa*). Malay likes to build its own words: *sejagat* (global), *antarabangsa*. The airport sign *Ketibaan Antarabangsa* = International Arrivals.

**Kena** means **have to, must** — one of the most useful words in spoken Malay. *Kena pulangkan* = have to return it, *kena bayar* = have to pay, *saya kena pergi* = I have to go. It also means "to be hit by, to get" (*kena denda* = get a fine), and both senses live side by side.
**Sebab** = because, the everyday word. *Sebab kena tukar* = because it has to be changed. *Kerana* is also correct and more formal.
**Mangga** here isn't the fruit — in Malay *mangga* also means **padlock**. The fruit is *mangga* too, and context tells them apart. A small, fun trap.

grammars.title: Question words
body: Malay questions are easier than English ones: you **don't swap** subject and verb, and there's no "do/does/did". The question word can go at the front or stay where the answer would be: *Awak nak apa?* = "You want what?" = What do you want?
after: ⚠️ **Bila** means **when** (a question). For "if" Malay uses **kalau**. (In Indonesian *bila* can also mean "if" — another subtle trap if you've met Indonesian.)

⚠️ **Macam mana** ("like which") is the everyday "how". *Bagaimana* is correct and appears in formal writing, but in speech almost everyone says *macam mana* — or, faster still, **camne**. *Macam mana nak pergi?* = "How do I get there?"

grammars.title: Ways to turn a sentence into a question
body: This is genuinely new. English changes the word order ("You are…" → "Are you…?"). Malay keeps the order and adds a marker — and which one you choose shows how formal you are.

head: Marker
Position
Example
Feel
rows: attached to the word in question

after: **Ke** and **tak** are the pair you'll hear most. The difference is subtle: *ke* asks **whether something is so** (*Awak pelajar ke?* = Are you a student?), while *tak* asks **yes or no, want or not** (*Nak makan tak?* = Want to eat or not?, *Ada duit tak?* = Got any money?). When in doubt, they can almost always be swapped without a mistake.

⚠️ Worth knowing: **a question with no softener can sound sharp.** *Awak buat apa?* in a flat voice can sound accusing. Add *-lah*, *ya* or a title, and the whole sentence changes: *Awak buat apa tu?* or *Encik nak ke mana ya?*

sections.title: Answering: yes, no and in between

head: Malay
English
Note
rows: *Kot* at the end of a sentence.

blocks.text: A Malay habit worth copying: **answer by repeating the verb**, not with "yes". Asked *Awak dah makan?* (Have you eaten?), the answer is *Dah* (already) — not *Ya*. Asked *Ada duit tak?*, the answer is *Ada* or *Takde*. It's like answering "Have you eaten?" with "I have"; in Malaysia it's practically the rule, and answering "yes" to everything sounds like a translation.

blocks.title: Softening a no
items: **Tak apalah.** — No thanks, it's fine. (turning down an offer politely)
**Saya tengok dulu.** — I'm just looking. (in a shop, to avoid pressure)
**Nanti saya beritahu.** — I'll let you know.
**Susah sikit.** — That's a bit difficult. (a gentle no)

⚠️ Saying no directly (*Tak nak.* = Don't want) isn't wrong, but without *-lah* or a smile it sounds firm. Malaysians say no in very roundabout ways, and recognizing a soft no matters as much as being able to say one.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right Malay question word.
Turn these formal questions into conversational ones (use *ke* or *tak*).
Answer the Malay way — repeat the verb, don't say "yes".

answers: Siapa — Bila — mana — Macam mana — Berapa — Kenapa
Awak pelajar baru ke? — Makanan ni sedap tak? — Awak nak ikut tak? — Ada wifi kat sini tak? — Awak faham tak?
Awak duduk kat mana? — Bila awak sampai? — Macam mana nak ke sana? — Boleh tolong saya tak? — Perkataan ni maksudnya apa? — Tandas kat mana ya?
Dah. — Takde. — Boleh. — Faham. — Tak nak.
